competitors.name: Social Science Statistics Pearson correlation calculator

weBeat: visual: a scatter in the user's own units with the best-fit line, a confidence band, one thin leave-one-out line per point, amber rings and labels on the points that move r by more than 0.1, zoom buttons, and a gauge on the -1 to +1 scale with the interval drawn as a bar; Pearson.com, correlationcoefficientcalculator.org and Stats Kingdom draw a scatter but none shows which point carries the correlation, and Omnicalculator, GigaCalculator and Social Science Statistics draw nothing

functional: 'Which point is carrying this?' table (r with each pair left out, flagged above 0.1), Pearson, Spearman and Kendall side by side with a plain note on when they disagree, 'What would it take' (smallest significant r, pairs needed for p below alpha and for 80% power, power for true correlations of 0.1, 0.3 and 0.5), a prediction from the line with the interval for the line and for one new point, testing against a correlation other than 0, weights, sentences in five styles, an 'Is Pearson appropriate' check, and the same example typed into Social Science Statistics and Stats Kingdom gave the same r, r squared, t, df and p as this page

every competitor feature kept except Matthews MCC, CSV / Excel file upload, PNG / PDF export, residual plot, the exact-distribution option, the Shapiro-Wilk normality test, R code, Print and last-run restore (dropped under his answers 'Approve all' and 'Add those, drop those (Recommended)', recorded in the parity file)
unverified: Copy buttons in a real clipboard session

GigaCalculator's Share and Embed buttons and correlationcoefficientcalculator.org's correlation matrix and dark-theme switch were seen but are not on this page (the matrix was named as a drop in the research report; share and embed were not named)
the Chicago-style sentence copies the pattern Social Science Statistics prints (r(8) = 0.70; p = .025); the style rule itself was not read
the strength words follow the scale Omnicalculator attributes to Evans (1996); the original was not read
power counts for 80% and the three power rows use the Fisher z approximation; checked against an independent implementation, not against another calculator

Omnicalculator, GigaCalculator, Pearson.com and correlationcoefficientcalculator.org were reopened after the build but only read, not typed into; Social Science Statistics and Stats Kingdom were typed into and gave the same r, t, df and p
